title: The Lifecourse GWAS Consortium
text:
The Lifecourse GWAS Consortium is an international collaboration led by researchers at the MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit, University of Bristol. It brings together 50 cohort studies and biobanks to investigate how genetic associations with complex traits vary across the lifecourse.
Genome-wide association studies commonly combine measurements collected at different ages and therefore implicitly assume that genetic associations remain constant over time. However, genetic variants may influence traits differently at different stages of life. The Lifecourse GWAS Consortium addresses this by generating harmonised, age-, sex- and ancestry-stratified genome-wide association results for 26 phenotypes measured from infancy to later adulthood.

Aim
The Consortium aims to investigate whether genetic associations vary systematically across the lifecourse and to improve understanding of the temporal genetic architecture of complex traits.


Objectives
The Consortium’s objectives are to:

Generate harmonised genome-wide association results for 26 anthropometric, cardiometabolic, inflammatory, respiratory, endocrine and other health-related phenotypes.
Conduct analyses at annual ages from infancy to 19 years, in five-year age groups across adulthood, and within broader life stages.
Examine genetic associations separately by sex and across European, African, East Asian, South Asian and admixed or other ancestry groups.
Combine results across contributing studies using methods that account for overlap between participants contributing measurements at different ages.
Identify genetic variants whose associations vary with age and model the timing and pattern of these changes across the lifecourse.
Group variants according to shared patterns of age-varying genetic association.
Investigate the biological and methodological drivers of age-varying genetic associations, including biological pathways, pleiotropy, selection bias and scale effects.
Evaluate how the predictive performance of polygenic risk scores varies across age, sex and ancestry.
Generate genetic instruments for downstream lifecourse Mendelian randomisation analyses examining whether the effects of selected exposures differ between life stages.



Participating studies and biobanks
The Consortium includes studies spanning childhood, adolescence and adulthood from Europe, North America, Asia and Australia. Together, they provide measurements across a wide range of ages and ancestral groups.

title: Projects
text:
The Consortium’s principal analysis examines how genetic associations with 26 phenotypes vary from infancy to later adulthood.


Participating studies use harmonised phenotype definitions and a centrally developed pipeline to conduct genome-wide association analyses stratified by:

Age or life stage
Sex
Ancestry

Analyses are conducted at annual ages from infancy to 19 years and in five-year age groups from age 20 onwards. Analyses are also conducted within broader life stages spanning birth, infancy and toddlerhood, early childhood, middle childhood, adolescence, young adulthood, middle adulthood and later adulthood.
Each phenotype and age or life-stage combination is analysed as a separate cross-sectional genome-wide association study. Participants with measurements at multiple ages can contribute to more than one age-specific analysis, but individual longitudinal trajectories are not modelled directly.
Study-specific results are quality controlled and combined through fixed-effects meta-analysis. Meta-analyses are conducted within European, African, East Asian, South Asian and admixed or other ancestry groups, as well as across all available ancestry groups.



The following 26 phenotypes are included:







Phenotype group
Phenotypes




Body size and composition
Body mass index; BMI-for-age z-score; height; waist circumference; waist-to-hip ratio; total body bone mineral density


Respiratory function
Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1); FEV1/FVC ratio


Blood pressure
Systolic blood pressure; diastolic blood pressure; pulse pressure


Lipids
LDL cholesterol; HDL cholesterol; triglycerides


Metabolic and inflammatory traits
C-reactive protein; interleukin 6; leptin; glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c); insulin; adiponectin


Nutritional and mineral traits
Calcium; vitamin D


Reproductive hormones
Oestradiol; total testosterone; bioavailable testosterone; sex hormone-binding globulin



Detailed definitions and preprocessing instructions are available in the phenotype definitions section of the analysis wiki.



Participating studies apply the central analysis pipeline to generate genome-wide association results for each available phenotype, age or life-stage, sex and ancestry stratum.
The pipeline standardises:

Phenotype preparation
Age and life-stage classification
Ancestry classification
Genetic quality control
Polygenic risk score analyses
Genome-wide association analyses

Instructions and code for cohort analysts are available through the Lifecourse GWAS analysis wiki.



Genome-wide significant variants are evaluated across age groups and life stages. Meta-regression is used to test whether their associations vary with age while accounting for overlap between participants contributing to different age-specific analyses.
Association patterns are then smoothed and clustered to identify groups of variants with similar age-varying profiles. These may include associations that increase, decrease, emerge or peak at particular stages of life.
Sensitivity analyses examine whether observed patterns could be influenced by methodological factors, including selection bias and scale effects.



Subsequent analyses will:

Compare age-varying genetic associations across sex and ancestry groups
Investigate functional enrichment and biological pathways
Examine pleiotropy among variants with age-varying associations
Evaluate the performance of polygenic risk scores across ages
Develop and evaluate life-stage-specific polygenic risk scores
Apply lifecourse Mendelian randomisation to selected exposure–outcome relationships




The harmonised cohort-level analysis pipeline has been implemented across participating studies. Age-, sex- and ancestry-stratified results are currently being quality controlled and combined through meta-analysis.

title: Projects
text:
Extension projects
The Consortium welcomes proposals for additional projects that build on its infrastructure, data and methods.
New or existing Consortium members wishing to propose an extension project should complete the project proposal form and submit it to the working group.
Proposals will be reviewed by the working group and steering committee for scientific relevance, feasibility and overlap with existing work. The lead of an approved project will be responsible for establishing an appropriate working group, delivering the research and ensuring that the contribution of the Lifecourse GWAS Consortium is appropriately recognised.
Further information about project leadership, authorship, software and data sharing is provided in the Consortium’s Principles of Collaboration.

title: Projects
text:
Data requests
Researchers from participating studies who wish to request access to emerging Consortium summary data should complete the early data request form.
Requests will be reviewed in accordance with the Consortium’s Principles of Collaboration and any restrictions imposed by contributing studies.
For questions about projects or data requests, please contact lifecourse-gwas-group@bristol.ac.uk.

Key papers


Morris, T. T., J. Heron, E. C. M. Sanderson, G. Davey Smith, V. Didelez, and K. Tilling. 2022. “Interpretation of Mendelian Randomization Using a Single Measure of an Exposure That Varies over Time.” Journal Article. Int J Epidemiol 51 (6): 1899–909. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyac136.


Power, G. M., E. Sanderson, P. Pagoni, A. Fraser, T. Morris, C. Prince, T. M. Frayling, et al. 2024. “Methodological Approaches, Challenges, and Opportunities in the Application of Mendelian Randomisation to Lifecourse Epidemiology: A Systematic Literature Review.” Journal Article. Eur J Epidemiol 39 (5): 501–20. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10654-023-01032-1.


Richardson, T. G., E. Sanderson, B. Elsworth, K. Tilling, and G. Davey Smith. 2020. “Use of Genetic Variation to Separate the Effects of Early and Later Life Adiposity on Disease Risk: Mendelian Randomisation Study.” Journal Article. BMJ 369: m1203. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.m1203.


Sanderson, E., T. G. Richardson, T. T. Morris, K. Tilling, and G. Davey Smith. 2022. “Estimation of Causal Effects of a Time-Varying Exposure at Multiple Time Points Through Multivariable Mendelian Randomization.” Journal Article. PLoS Genet 18 (7): e1010290. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1010290.
